rv.q: Its a gripping revival that proves theres plenty of life in Clifford Odetss half-forgotten American tragedy.
It’s a bluntly brilliant satire of capitalism and the way it destroys people who mess with it – chewing them up like drunks who’ve become heedlessly entangled in an escalator.
It’s a curiously anachronistic touch in a production that has lots of muscle, but throws too many loose punches.
The last 20 minutes go slightly off the rails as the production's melodramatic denouement resorts to explosive bursts of shouting and recrimination following a bloody and tragic bout.

Odets funded his stage plays by writing Hollywood film scripts, in an era when, alongside the classics fondly remembered today, countless other fair-to-middling melodramas were churned out and then forgotten. Golden Boy does feel like it could fit into that category, though it’s easy to see why it succeeded when it made its stage debut.
This is a production that packs a powerful punch, resulting in what is confidently a knockout hit.
I love a boxing noir with its fast wise-cracking dialogue, and thought this was terrific.

cn.t: O'Connor delivers a compelling performance in this Odets revival, with Daniel Mays earning particular praise, though critics note the play's dated moral simplicity undermines an otherwise stylish production with strong performances all around.
